finding.title: Reward token theft via transferFrom allowance
finding.description: The claim function calls rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, r) without checking whether rewardToken is the same contract as stakeToken. If an attacker deploys the staking contract with stakeToken == rewardToken (or a malicious token that returns true from transfer while executing arbitrary logic), they can exploit the update modifier's reentrancy or simply drain the reward balance because the contract holds an allowance on the stake token via stakeToken.transferFrom in stake(). More directly, since stake() uses transferFrom on stakeToken, if stakeToken == rewardToken the contract accumulates an allowance from users; claim() then transfers reward tokens (the same token) out, but the real issue is that there is no separation between staked and reward assets, allowing a single malicious token to act as both and break the accounting assumptions. In the specific deployed scenario, an attacker who convinces users to stake a token that is also the reward token can have their staked balance drained because withdraw() calls stakeToken.transfer(msg.sender, amt) and claim() calls rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, r); if both are the same token, the contract's balance of that token is the only limit, and there is no protection against the contract paying out more than it should from the pooled balance.
finding.attack: Deploy StakeRewards with stakeToken = rewardToken = maliciousToken. Have victim call stake(100e18), which executes stakeToken.transferFrom(victim, contract, 100e18), moving victim's tokens into the contract. Attacker then calls claim() (or withdraw()) to extract tokens from the shared pool. Because both functions transfer the same token from the contract, the attacker can withdraw reward tokens that are actually the victim's staked principal, or drain the contract's entire balance of that token.

patch.note: Added a constructor require that stakeToken and rewardToken must be different addresses. When they are the same token, the contract's single token pool mixes staked principal with reward payouts, so claim() can pay out staked principal (or drain the pool) because there is no separation between staked and reward assets. This is the smallest change that closes the attack vector while preserving normal behaviour for distinct stake/reward tokens.

finding.title: Missing zero checks on rewardRate and totalStaked division
finding.description: rewardPerToken() divides by totalStaked. If totalStaked is zero the function returns early, but if totalStaked becomes non-zero and later returns to zero via withdrawals while rewardPerTokenStored is non-zero, subsequent calls with totalStaked == 0 return the stored value, which is acceptable. However, rewardRate can be set to zero in the constructor, causing rewards to never accrue (not a vulnerability but a misconfiguration). The real high issue is that rewardRate is immutable and set at construction; if set extremely high, rewardPerToken() can overflow or produce astronomical values when multiplied by 1e18 and (block.timestamp - lastUpdate), though uint256 overflow is unlikely with realistic time deltas. More concretely, there is no validation that rewardRate > 0, and no cap, allowing a deployer to create a contract that pays out rewards faster than the rewardToken balance can support, causing claim() to revert on transfer due to insufficient contract balance, effectively locking the contract.
finding.attack: Deploy StakeRewards with rewardRate = 1e36 (or any value such that rewardRate * time * 1e18 exceeds the rewardToken balance held by the contract). A user stakes and waits; claim() computes a reward r larger than the contract's rewardToken balance, and rewardToken.transfer(msg.sender, r) reverts, permanently blocking claims for all users until more tokens are deposited (which may be impossible if only the deployer can mint).

finding.title: Staked balance updated before token transfer, allowing reentrancy/transferFrom front-run
finding.description: stake() increments staked[msg.sender] and totalStaked before calling stakeToken.transferFrom(). If the stakeToken is a malicious ERC20 with a reentrant transferFrom hook, the token contract can call back into the Staking contract (e.g., claim() or withdraw()) during the transferFrom execution. Because staked[msg.sender] is already inflated, the reentrant call can claim rewards on a balance that has not actually been settled yet, or withdraw more than was genuinely deposited, leading to reward inflation or theft of reward tokens.
finding.attack: Attacker creates a malicious token where transferFrom(from, to, amount) reenters the Staking contract by calling claim() or withdraw() on behalf of msg.sender. Victim calls stake(100e18) with the malicious token. Inside transferFrom, the reentrant claim() executes update(msg.sender), computing rewards based on the already-incremented staked[msg.sender] (100e18) even though the underlying token transfer may not have completed or may be reverted later. The attacker extracts unearned rewards. Alternatively, the malicious token's transferFrom reverts after the state update, leaving staked[msg.sender] and totalStaked inflated with no corresponding tokens in the contract, allowing the attacker to withdraw reward tokens against phantom staked balance.

finding.title: MockToken lacks balance underflow protection
finding.description: MockToken.transfer() and transferFrom() perform balance subtractions without require checks. In Solidity 0.8.x this causes an underflow revert if balance is insufficient, which is safe, but the absence of allowance checks in transferFrom() means any spender can transfer any amount from any caller without approval (allowance is decremented but never checked against the requested amount). This allows unlimited token theft from users who have approved the Staking contract, because the Staking contract calls stakeToken.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amt); if MockToken is used as stakeToken, a malicious actor could call MockToken.transferFrom(victim, attacker, hugeAmount) directly since allowance is not enforced, draining victim balances.
finding.attack: Attacker calls MockToken.transferFrom(victim, attacker, type(uint256).max) directly. Because transferFrom does not check allowance[f][msg.sender] >= a, the subtraction underflows (revert in 0.8.x) — actually in 0.8.x it reverts, so this is not exploitable for theft. However, if the MockToken is used with a compiler version below 0.8.0, this would silently underflow. Given pragma ^0.8.24, underflow reverts. The real issue is that transferFrom decrements allowance without checking it, but since it reverts on underflow, no funds are lost. This finding is low confidence for actual exploit under 0.8.24, but the missing checks are a latent issue if the pragma is ever lowered.
